steps.title: Acid
steps.body: A substance that produces H⁺ ions when dissolved in water. Acids have a pH below 7.

steps.title: Base
steps.body: A substance that neutralises an acid, producing a salt and water. Metal oxides, metal hydroxides and metal carbonates are bases.

steps.title: Alkali
steps.body: A base that dissolves in water, producing OH⁻ ions. Alkalis have a pH above 7.

steps.title: Neutralisation
steps.body: The reaction between an acid and a base to produce a salt and water only.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Method Reactants Products Notes Acid + metal Metal + acid Salt + hydrogen Only works with metals above hydrogen. Add metal until no more reacts (excess), then filter. Acid + base (insoluble) Metal oxide/hydroxide + acid Salt + water Add base until in excess (no more dissolves), then filter off excess solid. Evaporate to crystallise. Acid + alkali (titration) Soluble base + acid Salt + water Must use titration because both are in solution — need to measure exact volumes. Use indicator to find end point. Rules for naming salts: The first part comes from the metal (or ammonia). The second part comes from the acid: hydrochloric acid → chloride, sulfuric acid → sulfate, nitric acid → nitrate. Worked Example 4: Making copper(II) sulfate Describe how to make pure, dry crystals of copper(II) sulfate from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. 1. steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Foundation Write the word equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. | Foundation What ion do all acids produce in water? What ion do all alkalis produce in water? | Higher Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation of nitric acid with potassium hydroxide.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water | Acids produce H⁺ ions. Alkalis produce OH⁻ ions. | HNO₃(aq) + KOH(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l). Ionic equation: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) (the ionic equation is the same for all neutralisations between strong acids and alkalis)

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: The ionic equation H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) works for ALL neutralisations between strong acids and alkalis To name a salt: the metal comes first, then the acid name gives the second part (HCl → chloride, H₂SO₄ → sulfate, HNO₃ → nitrate) In making salts: use excess base method for insoluble bases (metal oxides), titration for soluble bases (alkalis) For precipitation questions, always give the ionic equation (only include the ions that form the precipitate) State symbols are important: (aq) for dissolved substances, (s) for precipitates and solid bases When describing salt-making methods, mention all steps including filtration, evaporation, crystallisation and drying
